source_document.body:
Warehouse leaders can’t predict every disruption , but they can prepare their facilities to adjust when plans fall apart. In this Q&A, Adam Brown , Senior Director for Market Intelligence at Dematic , discusses how simulation and flexible automation can help, and when it makes sense to rethink facility locations and inventory storage.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: You can’t plan for every disruption. So what makes a warehouse ready to handle something nobody saw coming?
Adam Brown: You can’t foresee every disruption, but you can prepare by identifying where your operation can adjust. If one piece of equipment goes down, can workflows adapt? If orders spike, do you know which part of the warehouse will reach its limit first? You may not know what the next disruption will be, but you can better understand how your operation is likely to respond.
That preparation goes beyond equipment. Employees need to know what to do when the normal process is interrupted, and backup plans need to be tested before anyone has to rely on them.
Software is a great solution to help teams spot trouble sooner. For example, Dematic Command Center brings together intelligence from across the system so teams can see where performance is slipping and what needs attention. That gives them time to act before a small issue becomes a bigger operational challenge.
RELATED STORIES: Before You Buy Warehouse Robots, Know What You’re Trying to Fix | Robots for the Rest of Us—Warehouse Automation Gets Easier
SC247: What’s a warning sign that a warehouse will struggle if demand suddenly jumps or the mix of orders changes?
Brown: A clear warning sign is when a relatively small change in demand creates a disproportionate increase in backlogs. If a modest jump in orders requires sustained overtime just to stay on schedule, the operation may not have room to absorb a larger disruption.
Order mix matters as much as total volume. A warehouse designed primarily to fulfill orders for retail stores may struggle when its order mix shifts toward e-commerce . Even if the overall number of units stays the same, the work required to fulfill those orders has changed.
Look at where work consistently piles up. That’s often where the right automation solution can make the biggest difference. Understanding those pressure points helps you choose the right approach, whether that means introducing more flexible automation or expanding an existing automated system. Planning for how that change affects the next step in the process helps the whole operation keep pace as demand grows.
SC247: For someone who hasn’t used a digital twin, how does it work, and what would you test first?
RELATED: Supply Chain 101: What Are Digital Twins and How Can They Benefit Your Company?
Brown: Think of a digital twin as a virtual version of your warehouse that uses intelligent operational data to help show how the facility behaves. It lets you test a change virtually before making it on the warehouse floor.
First, I’d make sure the model accurately reflects normal warehouse operations. Then I’d run a scenario the team recently experienced and compare the model’s results with what actually happened. Those checks help establish if the model is a reliable starting point for testing future disruptions.
Then I’d test a situation the team is concerned about. What happens if a key piece of equipment goes down during a busy shift? Can the backup process handle the work, or does it create a bottleneck somewhere else? That’s much better to find out in a model than with customer orders waiting to ship .
Adam Brown
SC247: Where can mobile robots and automated guided vehicles help an existing warehouse adjust, and where do they have limits?
Brown: Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) can automate repetitive movement between warehouse areas. Depending on the application, they can reduce employee travel or bring inventory directly to picking stations. They can also introduce automation in phases.
However, all technologies have limits. The vehicles need room to move, and their ability to navigate depends on the technology they use and conditions on the warehouse floor, including traffic and obstacles.
Adding more robots will make operations more efficient, but it won’t keep increasing output if other parts of the operation, such as picking, packing or shipping, can’t handle the additional volume. At some point, traffic can become a problem, or the receiving workstation may not be able to keep up. Automation aims to improve how goods move through the warehouse. The number of robots is only one part of that.
“Adding more robots will make operations more efficient, but it won’t keep increasing output if other parts of the operation, such as picking, packing or shipping, can’t handle the additional volume.”
SC247: How do you decide whether to change an existing warehouse, add another location, or rethink where you keep inventory?
Brown: Start by identifying what is limiting your business . A facility that lacks storage space presents a different problem than a distribution network that puts inventory too far from customers.
If the location still serves the business well, evaluate how much more capacity the existing facility can handle. Improving workflows or upgrading selected systems may create capacity without the cost of another building. High-density storage can also help when space is the main issue, provided it fits the building and the products being stored.
Sometimes the building is limiting business growth, or the business needs to serve customers in a different region. A new facility gives you more freedom to design around those needs, but it requires a larger investment and a longer timeline.
Putting inventory closer to customers can shorten delivery times. Existing brick-and-mortar stores are increasingly serving as mini-warehouses, supporting store replenishment and e-commerce fulfillment while keeping shipping costs competitive. However, they can also increase costs and require more stock across the network. You need to weigh that cost against the service improvement. The best choice should solve today’s problem and still make sense as the business grows.
SC247: How do you make the case for spending money on flexibility when the payoff might not come until something goes wrong?
“You don’t always need a major upgrade to be better prepared. Flexible automation also lets you start with one process and expand as your needs grow and your budget allows. Whether you’re fixing a recurring problem or introducing automation, a targeted investment can give the team time back now and take some pressure off when demand picks up.”
Brown: Investing in flexibility isn’t just about preparing for the future. You should determine how the investment can improve operations today. For example, reducing the time employees spend walking between tasks can improve daily productivity. It can also help the team manage a busier period with the people available. The same thinking applies to adding capacity in stages. A business can invest in what it needs now while leaving room to expand, rather than paying upfront for capacity it may not use for years.
Then put some numbers around the disruption you’re trying to prepare for. What would another week of overtime cost? What happens if orders can’t ship on time? How much does downtime impact your bottom line? Comparing those scenarios gives leaders a clearer sense of how much flexibility is worth paying for.
SC247: If a warehouse leader has a tight budget, what’s one practical change you’d suggest making now to prepare for the next disruption?
Brown: Start with a focused review of the part of the operation that most often slows everything else down. Look at recent stoppages and recurring jams to understand what is causing the lost time.
The answer may be a maintenance adjustment or a change in how work is released. If equipment failure is the concern, check that the right replacement part is available and employees know how to get the system running again.
You don’t always need a major upgrade to be better prepared. Flexible automation also lets you start with one process and expand as your needs grow and your budget allows. Whether you’re fixing a recurring problem or introducing automation, a targeted investment can give the team time back now and take some pressure off when demand picks up.
Adam Brown is Senior Director for Market Intelligence at Dematic
